doc.title: Ray Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Freelance studio system, quotas, contracts and scale
summary: He describes the shift from house-band contracts to freelancing, benefits, and radio scale of about $35.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: So, being a studio musician, you go to work in the studio—

Well it was all freelance when I — just when I got into it, they had contracts. Up until then, where they had house bands, all studios had their own group. And during that period I was doing radio. I did “The Phil Harris Show,” and I’m trying to think of what shows I did, and I started to do records, and there was also quotas, if you did movie studio work, you could only do a certain number of records, you couldn’t do radio at all I don’t think. They tried to divide up the work among all. So I was like in that field, doing radio. And records. And then the contracts went out and it got to be everything was freelance. And that’s when I started to get calls, to do picture calls. But I’ve always loved the idea that I never had a — because that was like going to an office, with those guys that were under contract to studios.
Did this give you any — this is like a 90s question — did you get health benefits and all that kind of stuff for that kind of work?

Not right away. It was, in fact it took a long time before they got that. But the scale was good. I mean compared to whatever other work there was, that was the best scale. And as I say with the contracts, you work on a yearly basis, whatever it was. You’d divide it up. That was guaranteed so much money a week. You signed up for a year. But anyhow when I got into it it was just — I don’t know exactly but I know compared to other work it was the highest per hour scale, I guess a three hour minimum calls.
Can you tell me what it was? Do you remember?
I don’t remember. I remember the radio shows were like $35, $36.
For a three hour session? © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
Well including the rehearsal and doing the show when I first started radio, I’m pretty sure that’s what it was.
Well that was decent money back then.
